title: Every Lesson Is a Promise
author: David Didau
summary: David Didau argues that a lesson is a series of promises to students, most of them unspoken: that everyone will answer questions, that no one can hide at the back, and that the teacher will return to a child who says 'I don't know'. Because working memory limits what a teacher can track across thirty children, those promises are broken constantly and often without notice. His remedy is the 'messy markbook', a seating plan on a clipboard marked with ticks for answers, dots for 'dunno', crosses for errors to revisit and stars for strong contributions. He credits Claire Woozley and Christine Counsell for the idea and shows how the same sheets can track whether the curriculum's larger promise of progress is being kept. Didau also takes on the belief that cold-calling harms anxious pupils, citing studies suggesting that frequent cold-calling raises comfort with discussion when teachers frame it as an invitation. The piece ends with a practical start-up routine and a candid answer to the workload objection.
points: Unvoiced classroom promises, such as returning to a child who says 'I don't know', shape whether students trust their teacher.
Limited working memory means teachers cannot reliably recall who has taken part, so the habit needs an external aid such as a seating plan on a clipboard.
A simple symbol system of ticks, dots, crosses and stars turns the markbook into a prompt for keeping each promise before the lesson ends.
Cold-calling framed as an invitation to think together, not a moral obligation, can raise rather than lower student comfort with discussion.
Messy markbooks kept over a term show whether the curriculum is working for particular children, provided they are never turned into an inspection document.
quotes: A lesson is a series of promises we make to students. Some of them we make out loud: “I’ll come back to you”, “Remind me about that at the end”, “That deserves a praise point”.

If I say I’ll come back to a student who can’t or won’t answer a question and then don’t, they learn that “I don’t know” works. If I keep going back to the same handful of keeners, everyone else learns that if they keep their heads down, they’ll be left alone.
Human memory and attention aren’t up to the job of keeping track of thirty children’s participation in a lesson.
The catch is that automatised habits tend to go unnoticed. If my habit is to always call on children with their hands up, I won’t necessarily know I’m doing it.
Saying, “It’s OK not to know, but I’ll come back to you,” is more likely to be perceived as an invitation rather than an ambush.
As the name suggests, a “messy” markbook isn’t meant to be inspected. If anyone asked to see it as evidence of something, the point would be lost.
Every lesson is a down payment on that promise, and a messy markbook is a tool for checking whether the payments are being made.
A messy markbook can’t make every student participate, but it will at least tell you who isn’t.
